extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies; researchers interested in political economy and ideology of news; advanced journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Critically analyze news content and news production to identify ideological patterns, elite influence, and institutional routines (e.g., propaganda filters, hegemony, source structures) that shape coverage. Applies theoretical frameworks (propaganda model, hegemony, Kuhnian paradigm, Hallin's spheres) and empirical methods (network analysis, close textual reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological mobilization tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Business class mobilizes to stave off public opinion and possible regulation by funding think tanks, economic reporting programs, awards and prizes for reporting, conferences and workshops between media and business executives, and advocacy ads (e.g., Mobil Oil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These strategies exploit journalists' professional occupational routines to further corporate ideology; they transcend any single firm's interests and address the needs of the business class generally (i.e., ideological mobilization). Use these categories to identify corporate attempts to shape media content and routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite news source structure / source cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether national media rely on a large, cohesive, interconnected group of elites (government officials, former officials, think-tank experts, key journalists) that span issues and programs, producing an 'insiders' group across shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use network analysis: consider sources 'linked' if they appear together on the same issue/story across programs (e.g., Nightline, MacNeil-Lehrer). A cohesive, interlocking web of sources supports elite-theory claims; little overlap supports a pluralist view. Source selection marks boundaries of political debate and reveals ideological assumptions behind news judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of network analysis to reveal source power
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources considered linked if they appear together with respect to the same issue or story across programs; mapping links over time yields a 'web' of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize source networks across programs and issues (e.g., appearance with Henry Kissinger links his co-guests indirectly). Empirically demonstrate whether a central insiders group cuts across issues and programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herman & Chomsky's five news filters (Propaganda Model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propaganda model includes five news 'filters': (1) the size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of the dominant mass media firms; (2) advertising as the primary income source of the mass media; (3) the reliance of the media on information provided by government, business, and 'experts' funded and approved by these primary sources and agents of power; (4) 'flak' as a means of disciplining the media; and (5) 'anticommunism' as a national religion and control mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these filters as diagnostic axes for evaluating systematic bias: ownership/ad revenue constraints, source dependence, disciplinary pressures (flak), and ideological control mechanisms (anticommunism). Look for how each filter shapes story choice, framing, volume, and quality of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source reliance as instrumental link to elites
rubrics_metrics.description: Media routines cause reliance on government and corporate sources because they can produce large quantities of authoritative news and corporations subsidize information gathering through PR budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate coverage by tracing the origin of factual material—government press offices, corporate PR—and assess how source convenience, authority, and material subsidy shape story content and constrains alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak as disciplinary mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Flak is negative responses to the media—complaints, threats, petitions, letters, articles—used to discipline and intimidate the media; often originates from the Right and is funded by foundations, think tanks, and media monitors (e.g., Accuracy in Media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify organized campaigns, monitors, and funded critics that generate flak; assess how fear of flak alters editorial choices or self-censorship, privileging elite-acceptable viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covert/state planting of favorable material ('White Propaganda')
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct planting of favorable news by government actors via secret collaboration with academics, contractors, consultants, prepared op-eds, coordinated visits through 'cut-outs', and consulting journalists to ensure favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of clandestine coordination (declassified memos, cut-outs, ghostwritten pieces) that shows direct state efforts to shape major media narratives; distinguish this from overt PR or official press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hegemony: media produce cohesive, commonsensical ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Hegemony refers to how ruling order maintains dominance: media institutions continually produce a cohesive ideology—a set of commonsensical values and norms—that reproduces and legitimates the social structure and causes subordinate classes to participate in their own domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how narratives make particular values seem 'natural' rather than coercive, how media absorb disparate values into consensus, and how repeated frames legitimize the status quo. Look for marginalization/delegitimation of voices outside elite circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative autonomy of media as source of legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because media have relative autonomy (not directly supervised by ruling powers), their messages gain greater legitimacy and credibility than if they were openly controlled, making hegemonic control more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bias, account for the paradox: less overt control can yield more persuasive ideological influence; examine institutional ties and routines rather than only formal censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines for the powerful / routines serving hegemonic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic routines (e.g., balancing, sourcing, reliance on officials) develop to meet hegemonic requirements as well as organizational needs; routines thus have ideological implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how everyday news practices function to reproduce hegemonic frames (e.g., who is considered a legitimate source, when balance is invoked, what counts as newsworthy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallin's spheres: consensus, legitimate controversy, deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic treatment varies by sphere: in consensus journalists act as advocates/celebrants; in legitimate controversy they seek balance; in deviance they expose, condemn, and exclude those outside political consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify issues/events into spheres to anticipate routines (e.g., balancing used in legitimate controversy but not in consensus or deviance). Use this to explain differential coverage and exclusion of radical viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing as routine and its ideological limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective routine of balancing sources is important only within the sphere of legitimate controversy; balancing formats prefer centrist or conservative experts and marginalize radical points of view, offering disagreement within an 'adequate comfort zone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect whether 'balance' actually frames middle-ground consensus and excludes substantive challenges. Watch for recurring formats that tokenise dissent without altering the overall frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: False balance and conflict-angle devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories may present opposing sides as numerically or rhetorically equal (false balance) despite disproportionate strength; conflict framing and juxtaposition (close-ups, soundbites, editing) can neutralize more substantive critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct close textual/visual analysis: compare raw footage to final packages, count attendance/sources vs. presented parity, examine choice and order of soundbites and images that create appearance of balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic linking in texts (e.g., pro-war = patriotism/support-the-troops)
rubrics_metrics.description: News texts can symbolically link a policy position to positive clusters (the troops, patriotism, community solidarity), thereby marginalizing critics by associating them with negative elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated associative language, editorial juxtaposition, and selection of individual stories (family members, anthems, flags) that tie policy support to culturally valued symbols; evaluate how critics are distanced from those symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: News paradigm (Kuhn) and exclusionary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalistic paradigm—an accepted model or pattern validated by consensus—focuses attention on some problems while excluding others; practitioners learn paradigms through practice rather than explicit rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the paradigm concept to identify which questions are considered legitimate; anomalies that don't fit the paradigm will be repaired or normalized. Assess how paradigmatic boundaries shape what counts as news or acceptable interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity, accuracy, balance, fairness as occupational norms with hegemonic function
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists invoke objectivity (or the more defensible 'accuracy', 'balance', 'fairness') and treat strongly held values as occupationally useless; deferring to elite sources is framed as objectivity while drawing conclusions from expertise is seen as bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate appeals to objectivity—who is presumed objective (insiders, official sources) and when 'bias' is attributed to individuals. Consider how these norms legitimize elite frames and exclude nonofficial perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' role in reinforcing paradigm and normalizing coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, having internalized journalistic norms, are considered less apt to succumb to bias and are more directly in touch with elite values; they are reluctant to break boundaries and may resist reporters who challenge elite frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing discrepancies between field reporting and institutional coverage, examine editorial gatekeeping, senior editors' contacts with elites, and how editors respond to reporter anomalies (e.g., rejecting pessimistic reporting from correspondents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local news as particularly effective ideological guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Local television, with a fragmented audience and emphasis on community symbols, amplifies cultural/economic imperatives (audience appeal, tabloid formats) and can produce ideologically coherent reporting supportive of government policy (e.g., 'support the troops').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze local news formats, emotional appeals, and community symbols to see how they construct consensus on national policies; pay attention to personalization (family members), visual symbolism, and appeals to community solidarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm violation and normalization (case studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a journalist violates the paradigm (e.g., A. Kent MacDougall's radical writing while a mainstream reporter), it prompts repair work and normalization by the institution to preserve hegemonic boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case studies of paradigm violations to see how organizations respond (discipline, public controversy, normalization). These instances reveal tacit boundaries and how occupational ideology enforces them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method: close reading of texts to identify ideological patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: In analyzing content for ideological patterns, combine close textual/visual reading with knowledge of routines and source structures to see how news combines and structures key elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform detailed comparisons (raw footage vs. final package), text/image juxtaposition, soundbite selection analysis, and cross-issue/source mapping to reveal framing, linkings, exclusions, and subtle ideological effects.
